questions.questionText: Your organization wants to retain Google Cloud logs for 5 years to meet regulatory compliance requirements. To minimize costs, which Google Cloud Logging feature and destination should you use?
options: Create a Log Router sink that exports logs to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Create a Log Router sink that exports logs to Cloud SQL.
Keep the logs in the default Cloud Logging bucket and extend the retention period to 5 years.
Create a Log Router sink that exports logs to Cloud Pub/Sub.
correctAnswers: Create a Log Router sink that exports logs to a Cloud Storage bucket.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Storage is the most cost-effective destination for long-term log archiving. By creating a Log Router sink, you can automatically export matching log entries to a Cloud Storage bucket, where you can also apply lifecycle policies (like moving to Archive storage) to further reduce costs.

why other options are wrong.Create a Log Router sink that exports lo: Cloud SQL is a relational database and is not a supported or cost-effective destination for Cloud Logging exports.
why other options are wrong.Keep the logs in the default Cloud Loggi: While you can create custom log buckets with longer retention, using Cloud Storage (especially Archive tier) is specifically designed and priced for long-term, low-cost compliance archiving.
why other options are wrong.Create a Log Router sink that exports lo: Pub/Sub is a messaging queue used for streaming logs to external systems, not for long-term storage.

questions.questionText: Your security team wants to run complex analytical queries using standard SQL on audit logs to investigate potential security incidents. Where should you export your logs to achieve this?

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery is Google Cloud's fully managed enterprise data warehouse. Exporting logs to BigQuery allows you to run complex, high-speed analytical queries on massive log datasets using standard SQL.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage: Cloud Storage is an object store for archiving. While you can query it using external tables, BigQuery is the native, high-performance destination for SQL log analysis.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Pub/Sub: Pub/Sub is a real-time messaging service, not a SQL database for querying historical logs.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Spanner: Cloud Spanner is a transactional relational database and is not a natively supported destination for Log Router exports.

questions.questionText: You are managing a fleet of Compute Engine virtual machines. You notice that while Cloud Monitoring automatically displays CPU utilization, it does not display the Memory (RAM) utilization or disk space usage of the instances. What must you do to collect these metrics?
options: Install the Google Cloud Ops Agent on the virtual machines.
Enable the 'Detailed Monitoring' flag in the Compute Engine console.
Create a VPC Firewall rule to allow traffic on port 443.
Upgrade the VMs to a larger custom machine type.
correctAnswers: Install the Google Cloud Ops Agent on the virtual machines.

explanation.general explanation: By default, Google Cloud can only monitor metrics visible from the hypervisor level (like CPU, network traffic, and basic disk I/O). To gather in-guest metrics like Memory (RAM) utilization, free disk space, and application logs, you must install the Google Cloud Ops Agent on the VM.

why other options are wrong.Enable the 'Detailed Monitoring' flag in: There is no simple flag to magically read guest memory without an agent installed inside the OS.
why other options are wrong.Create a VPC Firewall rule to allow traf: Firewall rules do not grant Google Cloud visibility into the guest operating system's RAM usage.
why other options are wrong.Upgrade the VMs to a larger custom machi: Changing the machine size does not change what metrics are collected.

questions.questionText: Which two of the following services are natively supported destinations for Cloud Logging Log Router sinks? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Logging allows you to route logs to specific supported destinations using Log Sinks. The natively supported external destinations are Cloud Storage (for archiving), BigQuery (for analytics), and Cloud Pub/Sub (for streaming to external SIEMs like Splunk).

why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL: Cloud SQL is a relational database and is not a supported destination for Log Router.
why other options are wrong.Memorystore for Redis: Memorystore is an in-memory caching service and cannot be used as a log sink destination.

questions.questionText: A critical Compute Engine instance was unexpectedly deleted yesterday. To investigate 'who' deleted the instance and 'when', which specific Google Cloud log should you examine?

explanation.general explanation: Admin Activity audit logs record API calls and administrative actions that modify the configuration or metadata of resources. Deleting a virtual machine is an administrative action that alters the system state, so it is recorded here.

why other options are wrong.Data Access Audit Logs: These record API calls that read the configuration or metadata of resources, as well as user-driven API calls that create, modify, or read user-provided data. They do not record resource deletion.
why other options are wrong.VPC Flow Logs: These logs record network traffic flows sent from and received by VM instances, not administrative actions.
why other options are wrong.System Event Audit Logs: These contain log entries for Google Cloud administrative actions that modify resources (like a live migration), but not actions initiated by a user.

questions.questionText: You want to ensure that your global e-commerce website is reachable and responding within 2 seconds to customers in North America, Europe, and Asia. Which Cloud Monitoring feature should you configure?

explanation.general explanation: Uptime checks verify the availability of your application by sending requests to it from multiple locations around the world (e.g., North America, Europe, Asia). You can configure them to alert you if the application fails to respond or responds too slowly.

why other options are wrong.Log-based Metrics: Log-based metrics create charts based on log entries, but they do not actively probe your external website's availability from global locations.
why other options are wrong.VPC Flow Logs: VPC Flow Logs capture internal network packet flows; they do not perform external availability polling.
why other options are wrong.Custom Dashboards: Dashboards visualize data, but Uptime Checks are the specific mechanism that actually probes the website.

questions.questionText: You want to be notified when the CPU utilization of any virtual machine in your Managed Instance Group exceeds 85% for more than 5 minutes. In Cloud Monitoring, what specifically defines this criteria?

explanation.general explanation: An Alerting Policy in Cloud Monitoring is made up of 'Conditions' and 'Notification Channels'. The Condition defines exactly what triggers the alert (e.g., CPU > 85% for 5 minutes).

why other options are wrong.Notification Channel: The Notification Channel defines *where* the alert is sent (e.g., email, SMS, Slack), not the threshold criteria.
why other options are wrong.Uptime Check Matcher: A matcher verifies if the response body of an Uptime Check contains specific text; it does not measure CPU utilization.
why other options are wrong.Log Exclusion Rule: An exclusion rule is used to stop specific logs from being ingested to save money, not for monitoring CPU metrics.

questions.questionText: Which two of the following are supported Notification Channels in Google Cloud Monitoring for receiving alerts when a system breaches its thresholds? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Monitoring supports a wide variety of notification channels to alert engineers when an incident occurs. Email, SMS, Webhooks, Slack, Pub/Sub, and 3rd party incident management tools like PagerDuty are natively supported.

why other options are wrong.Twitter Direct Message: Twitter (X) is not a supported enterprise incident management notification channel.
why other options are wrong.WhatsApp: WhatsApp is not natively supported as a notification channel in Cloud Monitoring.

questions.questionText: Your application has an internal queue. You want to monitor the exact number of items currently waiting in this internal application queue. Because this is application-specific data, Google Cloud does not collect it automatically. How can you send this data to Cloud Monitoring?
options: Create a Custom Metric and write code to push the data to the Monitoring API.
Install the standard Ops Agent, which automatically detects application queues.
Configure an Uptime Check to poll the queue.
Create a System Event log sink.
correctAnswers: Create a Custom Metric and write code to push the data to the Monitoring API.

explanation.general explanation: Custom metrics allow you to record application-specific data that Cloud Monitoring does not collect by default. You define the custom metric and use the Cloud Monitoring API (or client libraries) within your application code to transmit the data (like queue length) to Google Cloud.

why other options are wrong.Install the standard Ops Agent, which au: The Ops Agent collects system metrics (RAM, disk) and standard third-party app metrics (like Apache/Nginx), but it cannot magically know about your proprietary internal application code logic.
why other options are wrong.Configure an Uptime Check to poll the qu: Uptime checks verify if an HTTP/TCP endpoint responds; they do not extract internal queue metrics.
System events track Google infrastructure events (like VM migrations), not application-level custom data.

questions.questionText: Your company has three Google Cloud projects (Dev, QA, and Prod). You want a single, centralized dashboard where your operations team can view the metrics and logs for all three projects simultaneously. What Cloud Monitoring feature enables this?

explanation.general explanation: A Metrics Scope defines the set of Google Cloud projects whose metrics are monitored by a single Cloud Monitoring workspace. By adding multiple projects to one Metrics Scope, you can create unified dashboards and alerts across all of them.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Trace: Cloud Trace is for latency tracing across microservices, not for grouping multiple projects into a single monitoring view.
why other options are wrong.VPC Peering: VPC Peering connects internal networks together; it does not unify monitoring dashboards.
why other options are wrong.Log Exclusion: Log exclusions are used to discard logs to save money, unrelated to multi-project monitoring.

questions.questionText: Your application writes a specific error string ('PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT') to Cloud Logging whenever a third-party API fails. You want to trigger a Cloud Monitoring alert whenever this error appears more than 10 times in a minute. How should you bridge Logging and Monitoring to achieve this?
options: Create a Log-based Metric for the error string, then create an Alerting Policy based on that metric.
Use the Cloud Trace API to scan the logs for timeouts.
Create a Cloud Pub/Sub topic and subscribe the billing team to it.
Configure an Uptime Check to look for the string in the system logs.
correctAnswers: Create a Log-based Metric for the error string, then create an Alerting Policy based on that metric.

explanation.general explanation: Log-based metrics allow you to extract data from Cloud Logging and convert it into numerical metrics in Cloud Monitoring. You can create a log-based metric that counts occurrences of 'PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT' and then attach a standard Alerting Policy to that newly created metric.

why other options are wrong.Use the Cloud Trace API to scan the logs: Trace tracks application latency, it does not scan raw text logs for custom string matches to trigger alerts.
why other options are wrong.Create a Cloud Pub/Sub topic and subscri: While Pub/Sub can export logs, it does not natively provide threshold counting and alerting. Monitoring is the correct tool.
why other options are wrong.Configure an Uptime Check to look for th: Uptime checks poll external HTTP/TCP endpoints; they cannot read internal log files.

questions.questionText: Your engineering team is overwhelmed by thousands of raw exception stack traces in Cloud Logging, making it difficult to identify the most frequent bugs. Which Google Cloud service automatically analyzes logs to group identical exceptions and alert developers to new application crashes?

explanation.general explanation: Error Reporting automatically counts, analyzes, and aggregates crashes and exceptions found in your application logs. It groups identical stack traces together, providing a clean dashboard of the most frequent bugs, and can notify you when a new, unseen error occurs.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Profiler: Profiler analyzes code performance (CPU/Memory usage), not application crashes or exceptions.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Audit Logs: Audit logs track administrative actions and API access, not application code exceptions.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy: IAP is an access control service, entirely unrelated to application logging.

questions.questionText: Google strongly recommends installing the unified 'Ops Agent' on your Compute Engine VMs instead of the legacy agents. Which two legacy agents does the Ops Agent replace? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: The Google Cloud Ops Agent is a single, unified agent that replaces the two older, separate legacy agents: the Cloud Logging agent (fluentd) and the Cloud Monitoring agent (collectd). It collects both logs and metrics in a single installation.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Trace agent: Cloud Trace is instrumented via SDK libraries in application code, not a legacy system agent replaced by the Ops Agent.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Profiler agent: Cloud Profiler is also instrumented directly into application code via profiling libraries, not replaced by the infrastructure Ops Agent.

questions.questionText: Your organization uses a third-party Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) tool, such as Splunk, hosted outside of Google Cloud. What is the standard Google Cloud architecture for continuously streaming Cloud Logging data to this external tool?
options: Create a Log Sink to export logs to Cloud Pub/Sub, then have the SIEM tool subscribe to the topic.
Create a Log Sink to export logs to Cloud SQL, and have the SIEM tool run SQL queries hourly.
Use the Ops Agent to email the logs to the SIEM tool.
Configure the SIEM tool to read directly from the local disk of each Compute Engine instance.
correctAnswers: Create a Log Sink to export logs to Cloud Pub/Sub, then have the SIEM tool subscribe to the topic.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub is a highly scalable, real-time messaging service. The standard practice for integrating Google Cloud logs with external third-party SIEM tools (like Splunk or Datadog) is to create a Log Sink that routes logs to a Pub/Sub topic, which the external tool then consumes in real time.

why other options are wrong.Create a Log Sink to export logs to Clou: Cloud SQL is not a supported log export destination, and batch querying is not a real-time streaming solution.
why other options are wrong.Use the Ops Agent to email the logs to t: Email is not an enterprise data streaming protocol.
why other options are wrong.Configure the SIEM tool to read directly: This bypasses centralized Cloud Logging entirely, is highly insecure, and is practically impossible to manage at scale.

questions.questionText: You just deployed a new Virtual Machine on Compute Engine and have not installed any agents on it yet. Which metric is Cloud Monitoring NOT able to track automatically?

explanation.general explanation: Without the Ops Agent, Google Cloud can only track metrics visible to the hypervisor (outside the VM). This includes CPU usage, Network traffic, and basic Disk I/O. Memory (RAM) utilization is an 'in-guest' metric and requires the Ops Agent to be installed inside the OS to track it.

why other options are wrong.CPU utilization: This is automatically tracked by the hypervisor without an agent.
why other options are wrong.Network bytes sent: This is automatically tracked by the hypervisor.
why other options are wrong.Disk read operations: This is automatically tracked by the hypervisor.

questions.questionText: Your networking team wants to monitor internal network packet traffic, including source and destination IP addresses and ports, between Compute Engine VMs. Which feature integrates with Cloud Logging to provide this visibility?

explanation.general explanation: VPC Flow Logs record a sample of network flows sent from and received by VM instances. These logs integrate with Cloud Logging and contain network metadata like source/destination IPs, ports, and protocols, making them essential for network monitoring and security analysis.

why other options are wrong.Admin Activity Audit Logs: These log administrative API calls (like creating a subnet), not the actual network packets flowing between VMs.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Trace: Trace maps application latency, not raw network packet flows.
why other options are wrong.Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) Logs: IAP logs track user access to web applications, not internal VM-to-VM network traffic.

questions.questionText: A compliance auditor wants proof of 'who accessed what data' in your Cloud Storage buckets. Which specific Cloud Audit Log tracks API calls that read user-provided data?

explanation.general explanation: Data Access audit logs record API calls that read the configuration or metadata of resources, as well as user-driven API calls that create, modify, or read user-provided data (such as querying a BigQuery table or downloading an object from Cloud Storage).

why other options are wrong.Admin Activity audit logs: These log actions that modify configuration or metadata (like creating a bucket), not who read the data inside the bucket.
why other options are wrong.System Event audit logs: These log Google-initiated system events (like a VM live migration), not user data access.
why other options are wrong.Policy Denied audit logs: These log when a user is denied access due to VPC Service Controls, but Data Access logs track successful reads.

questions.questionText: You notice in Cloud Logging that several of your Compute Engine instances were subjected to a 'Live Migration' maintenance event. Which type of audit log records these actions performed by Google's systems rather than by your users?

explanation.general explanation: System Event audit logs contain log entries for Google Cloud administrative actions that modify the configuration of resources, but are initiated by Google's systems (like maintenance events and live migrations), rather than by direct user action.

why other options are wrong.Admin Activity audit logs: These log administrative actions initiated by human users or your service accounts, not Google's internal maintenance systems.
why other options are wrong.Data Access audit logs: These log who read your data, not system maintenance events.
why other options are wrong.VPC Flow Logs: These log network traffic, not infrastructure maintenance events.

questions.questionText: When creating a user-defined log-based metric in Google Cloud, which two types of metrics can you create? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Logging supports two types of user-defined log-based metrics: Counter metrics (which count the number of log entries matching a given filter) and Distribution metrics (which accumulate numeric data from log entries, like latencies or payload sizes, into buckets).

why other options are wrong.Gauge metric: While a gauge is a standard metric type in Cloud Monitoring, it is not a type you can natively create as a log-based metric from text logs.
why other options are wrong.Heatmap metric: A heatmap is a visualization chart type in dashboards, not a fundamental log-based metric type.

questions.questionText: By default, how long does Google Cloud Logging retain Admin Activity audit logs in the standard _Required log bucket?

explanation.general explanation: By default, Google Cloud retains Admin Activity audit logs, System Event audit logs, and Access Transparency logs for 400 days in the _Required log bucket. This long retention ensures robust security auditing capabilities.

why other options are wrong.30 days: This is the default retention period for Data Access audit logs and most other standard logs in the _Default bucket, but Admin Activity logs are kept much longer.
why other options are wrong.Indefinitely: Google Cloud does not store logs indefinitely for free by default. You must export them to Cloud Storage for indefinite archiving.

questions.questionText: An Alerting Policy in Cloud Monitoring triggered an incident yesterday because CPU usage spiked. Today, the CPU usage has returned to normal levels. What happens to the incident state in Cloud Monitoring?
options: The incident automatically resolves and closes.
The incident remains open until a human acknowledges it.
The incident is deleted from the history entirely.
The incident is forwarded to Error Reporting.
correctAnswers: The incident automatically resolves and closes.

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud Monitoring, alerting policies are stateful. When the condition that triggered the alert is no longer met (e.g., CPU drops back below the threshold), Cloud Monitoring automatically resolves and closes the incident.

why other options are wrong.The incident remains open until a human: While a human can acknowledge an open incident, if the condition stops being true, the system will auto-resolve it regardless.
why other options are wrong.The incident is deleted from the history: Closed incidents remain in the history for auditing and postmortem purposes; they are not deleted.
why other options are wrong.The incident is forwarded to Error Repor: Error Reporting tracks code exceptions, not resolved CPU metric alerts.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a distributed microservices application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to discover why certain user requests take too long by tracking the requests as they hop from one microservice to another. Which Google Cloud observability tool is built for this?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Trace is a distributed tracing system that collects latency data from your applications. It shows how requests propagate through your microservices architecture, highlighting the exact service causing latency bottlenecks.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Profiler: Profiler analyzes CPU and memory consumption within the application code, not the end-to-end request latency across multiple services.
why other options are wrong.VPC Flow Logs: VPC Flow Logs track network packet data, not application-level HTTP request tracing.
why other options are wrong.Error Reporting: Error Reporting aggregates crashes and exceptions, not latency delays.

questions.questionText: Your code is running slower than expected and consuming excessive amounts of RAM on the server. You want to visually identify which specific functions in your code are the most resource-intensive. Which tool provides a visual 'flame graph' to show this?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Profiler is a continuous CPU and memory profiling tool. It captures resource usage in your production code and displays it in a visual flame graph, making it easy to identify which specific functions are consuming the most CPU or RAM.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Trace: Trace shows latency across services, but not function-level CPU or RAM consumption.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Logging: Logging captures text-based event records, not continuous code performance profiling.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Build: Cloud Build is a CI/CD tool, not a performance profiling tool.

questions.questionText: Data Access audit logs can generate massive amounts of log data because they record every single read and write. By default, how long does Cloud Logging retain Data Access audit logs in the _Default bucket?

explanation.general explanation: By default, logs routed to the _Default log bucket (which includes Data Access audit logs, if enabled) are retained for 30 days. This shorter retention period prevents runaway costs from high-volume logs.

why other options are wrong.400 days: This is the default retention for Admin Activity and System Event logs in the _Required bucket, but not for Data Access logs.
why other options are wrong.1 year: This is incorrect, though you can configure custom retention up to 3650 days if you choose to pay for it.

questions.questionText: Which two of the following are distinct categories of Cloud Audit Logs provided by Google Cloud? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud provides several specific categories of Cloud Audit Logs: Admin Activity, Data Access, System Event, and Policy Denied. These logs help security and compliance teams answer 'who did what, where, and when'.

why other options are wrong.Firewall Rule Audit Logs: Firewall rules generate network logs (Firewall Rules Logging), but they are not an official category of 'Cloud Audit Logs'.
why other options are wrong.Application Exception Logs: These are application-level logs handled by Error Reporting, not administrative Cloud Audit Logs.

questions.questionText: You want to visually combine the CPU utilization metric of a VM, the number of incoming HTTP requests to a Load Balancer, and the length of a Pub/Sub queue onto a single screen for your operations team. What should you create?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Monitoring Custom Dashboards allow you to create charts and graphs that combine various metrics from multiple Google Cloud services onto a single visual pane of glass for operational monitoring.

why other options are wrong.A Cloud Logging Sink: Sinks route log data to destinations; they do not visualize numeric metrics.
why other options are wrong.A Cloud Trace timeline: Trace visualizes the latency of a single request across services, not general operational metrics like CPU or queue length.
why other options are wrong.An Error Reporting group: Error reporting groups identical crashes, not operational metric charts.

questions.questionText: Your application generates a massive volume of 'INFO' level logs. These logs are useful for debugging but are costing your company too much money in Cloud Logging storage fees. What is the best way to stop these specific logs from being ingested into Cloud Logging while still allowing 'ERROR' logs to pass through?
options: Create a Log Exclusion rule in the Log Router.
Delete the Cloud Logging API from the project.
Configure an Alerting Policy to delete INFO logs.
Lower the metric retention period to 1 day.
correctAnswers: Create a Log Exclusion rule in the Log Router.

explanation.general explanation: Log Exclusions allow you to filter out specific log entries (e.g., severity='INFO') at the Log Router level so they are never ingested into Cloud Logging buckets. This prevents them from generating storage costs while allowing higher severity logs (like ERRORs) to be retained.

why other options are wrong.Delete the Cloud Logging API from the pr: This would break all logging entirely, including critical security and error logs.
why other options are wrong.Configure an Alerting Policy to delete I: Alerting policies send notifications; they do not manage log ingestion or deletion.
why other options are wrong.Lower the metric retention period to 1 d: Metrics retention is handled separately from log retention, and lowering log retention globally doesn't solve the ingestion volume issue.

questions.questionText: You configured an Uptime Check to verify that your website is available. The check indicates the website is 'Up' because it receives an HTTP 200 response, but the page is actually displaying a blank white screen. How can you configure the Uptime Check to verify the page content is actually rendering correctly?
options: Add a Content Matcher to the Uptime Check.
Create a Log-based metric for the blank screen.
Enable Cloud Trace on the Uptime Check.
Increase the frequency of the Uptime Check to 1 minute.
correctAnswers: Add a Content Matcher to the Uptime Check.

explanation.general explanation: A Content Matcher allows an Uptime Check to look for a specific string of text in the HTTP response body (e.g., 'Welcome to our store'). If the text is missing (like on a blank white screen), the check fails even if the HTTP status code is 200 OK.

why other options are wrong.Create a Log-based metric for the blank: A blank screen is a visual state on the frontend; it doesn't necessarily write an error to the backend logs to create a metric from.
Trace measures latency, not HTML content validation.
why other options are wrong.Increase the frequency of the Uptime Che: Checking more often won't change the fact that the check thinks a blank page returning HTTP 200 is healthy.

questions.questionText: The Google Cloud Ops Agent is the primary tool for collecting telemetry from Compute Engine instances. Which two operating system families does the Ops Agent officially support? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: The Google Cloud Ops Agent is officially supported on both Linux and Windows Server environments running on Compute Engine virtual machines. It collects standard system metrics and logs natively for both OS families.

why other options are wrong.macOS: Google Cloud does not offer macOS Compute Engine VMs, and the agent does not support it.
why other options are wrong.ChromeOS: ChromeOS is an end-user client operating system, not a server OS for Compute Engine.

questions.questionText: An Alerting Policy triggers an incident and sends an email to the operations team. A team member opens the email and clicks the 'Acknowledge' button in the Cloud Console. What does this action do?
options: It marks the incident as being investigated but does not resolve the incident.
It automatically resolves the incident and stops all monitoring.
It triggers a script to reboot the affected virtual machine.
It deletes the alert policy entirely to prevent duplicate emails.
correctAnswers: It marks the incident as being investigated but does not resolve the incident.

explanation.general explanation: Acknowledging an incident in Cloud Monitoring signals to the rest of the team that someone is actively looking into the problem. It suppresses further reminder notifications, but it does not resolve or close the incident. The incident will only close when the underlying metric returns to a healthy state.

why other options are wrong.It automatically resolves the incident a: Resolving happens automatically when the metric recovers; acknowledging just means a human is working on it.
why other options are wrong.It triggers a script to reboot the affec: Acknowledging is a state change in the monitoring dashboard, not an automation trigger for VM reboots.
why other options are wrong.It deletes the alert policy entirely to: Deleting the policy would disable future monitoring, which is not the function of acknowledging an alert.
